Work  /  IDEXX — Pet Health Network
IDEXX · Brand creation · Naming · Digital

Built to be a test. Still running fourteen years later.

IDEXX needed to reach pet owners directly for the first time in its history. Pet Health Network was how the company found out whether that would work — and it never had to be replaced.

Client

IDEXX Laboratories (NASDAQ: IDXX)

Services

Brand creation, naming, visual identity, digital

Brand created

2011

Launched

July 2012 · live today

A pet owner, at home, on the thing IDEXX built to reach them. The cat is not part of the brief.

The challenge

IDEXX is a Fortune 1000 diagnostics company whose customers are veterinarians. Its products are analyzers and lab services — equipment a pet owner never sees and could not evaluate.

The company wanted to reach those owners directly for the first time. That is a real risk for an established B2B brand: go straight to consumers under the corporate name, and a soft reception damages the name that sells the analyzers. The work was not just to design a service. It was to give IDEXX a way to find out, without betting the parent brand on the answer.

The approach

Launch it under its own name. Pet Health Network was built as a brand a pet owner would trust on its own terms — an educational resource with pet care articles and practice websites, plus a communication tool connecting veterinarians to their clients before, during and after a visit.

The naming did the strategic work. Pet put the owner first, not the practice. Health set it against the commercial content that fills the category. Network promised something bigger than one clinic’s newsletter. None of it required knowing who IDEXX was — which was the point.

The identity was built in 2011. IDEXX then tested it — a beta across 120 veterinary clinics — before the public launch in July 2012. Work that survives that much scrutiny before it reaches an audience is work that was right early.

“I’ve never seen that kind of pickup, that fast, in the industry — ever.”

Jonathan Ayers, then CEO, IDEXX Laboratories — on the July 2012 launch
The mark — four paw prints, a name an owner can trust without knowing who owns it — and the chart their vet handed them. “How old is your pet in people years?” answers a question every owner already has, then turns the answer into a conversation about senior care.

Into the practice, and onto the screen

The system extended past print. Appointment cards in four color variants so a practice could pick one that suited its own look, and a results email that did the thing the whole venture existed for — put a diagnostic outcome in front of an owner in language they could act on.

“We’re excited to see you” and “Good News! The results are in: your pet is healthy.” Diagnostics, delivered as reassurance.

Built to be handed over

Every piece had to work in the two minutes a veterinarian has at the end of an appointment. Named pets on the covers rather than stock animals — Phantom, 2012; Bailey & Sebastian — so an owner sees a patient rather than a category.

Inside, the clinical material is laid out the way a worried owner reads it: what to watch for, how the diagnosis is made, what treatment looks like, what you can do. Anatomical illustration where a photograph would not explain enough.

Cover and interior. The heart diagram earns its place — it is the one thing a photograph cannot do.

One system, any topic

The brochure was a template rather than a piece. Medical imaging, blood work, pancreatitis, feline heart disease — the same structure absorbing whatever the practice needed to explain next, without a redesign each time.

Four titles, one system. The reason a company keeps using something.

The outcome

Owners responded. The services became IDEXX’s first cloud offerings aimed at pet owners and its fastest-growing business segment, and the brand was brought fully inside the company rather than retired.

Fourteen years on, Pet Health Network is still an IDEXX service. Most brand work is replaced within a few years. This one was adopted.
